title: Quantum oscillations and Dirac dispersion in tunable kagome lattice Lu$_{1-y}$Y$_y$(Nb$_{1-x}$Ta$_x$)$_6$Sn$_6$
authors: Keenan Avers, Phineas Sobel, Lochlan Joyce, Jared Dans, Prathum Saraf, Ram Kumar, Shanta Saha, Peter Zavalij, Johnpierre Paglione
abstract: Kagome lattice crystal systems present interesting symmetry-protected band structure features such as flat bands, van Hove singularities, and linearly dispersing Dirac/Weyl points that provide a rich playground for strongly correlated electron physics. Motivated by the rich properties and charge density wave evolution through the 1-6-6 series of compounds, we present our results in single crystal growth and characterization of the of Lu$_{1-y}$Y$_y$(Nb$_{1-x}$Ta$_x$)$_6$Sn$_6$ double-alloy system, including evolution of the charge density wave transition, electrical transport behavior and resultant phase diagrams. Using a novel growth technique, the synthesis of high quality crystals with extended length along the crystallographic $c$-axis allows us to follow the gradual suppression of charge density wave (CDW) order with Y substitution, and observe quantum oscillations in both magnetoresistance and magnetization throughout the series. We review the evolution of Fermi surfaces, effective masses and quasiparticle dispersion through the alloy series, revealing a decrease in size of Fermi surfaces that trends with both substitutions, and a scaling between effective mass and Fermi wavevector that suggests a regime with Dirac-like dispersion. The ability to fine-tune crystallographic, ground state and electronic dispersion properties of the \lit\ system with minimal impact of disorder opens a path torward further understanding the nature of the kagome lattice and its novel states and interactions.
summary: This work reports on the synthesis and characterization of tunable kagome lattice compounds ($	ext{Lu}_{1-y}	ext{Y}_y(	ext{Nb}_{1-x}	ext{Ta}_x)_6	ext{Sn}_6$). By measuring quantum oscillations, the researchers map out how alloying tunes the Fermi surface topology and tracks its evolution relative to a competing Charge Density Wave (CDW) order. This demonstrates fine control over novel electronic states in correlated materials.
main_problem: The study investigates quantum oscillations and Dirac dispersion in a tunable kagome lattice system to understand its rich electronic properties.
main_result: The research reveals that the Fermi surface size and effective mass evolve systematically across the alloy series, suggesting a transition towards or proximity to Dirac-like band dispersion. The interplay between this electronic structure and Charge Density Wave (CDW) order is mapped out.
method: The authors employed single crystal growth of double-alloyed compounds and characterized them using electrical transport measurements (magnetoresistance) and magnetization measurements, analyzing quantum oscillations via the Lifshitz–Kosevich theory.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{Lu}_{1-y}	ext{Y}_y(	ext{Nb}_{1-x}	ext{Ta}_x)_6	ext{Sn}_6$ double-alloy, which possesses a kagome lattice structure known for hosting flat bands and Dirac/Weyl points.
key_observables: Quantum oscillation frequencies ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$), effective masses ($m_i$), Fermi surface size changes, Charge Density Wave (CDW) transition temperature evolution, and magnetoresistance anisotropy.
important_parameters: Compositional tuning via Y substitution ($y$) and Ta alloying ($x$); low temperatures ($T \approx 2	ext{ K}$); magnetic field dependence ($B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting quantum oscillation data to the Lifshitz–Kosevich equation, and it assumes that changes in Fermi surface size are due to competing interactions rather than simple doping.
figures_summary: Figures show resistivity vs. magnetic field confirming large magnetoresistance and SdH oscillations; plots track CDW signatures ($ho$ minima/kinks) as a function of Y concentration; FFT spectra map the evolution of multiple oscillation frequencies with composition.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents structural characterization, followed by transport measurements to observe CDW transitions. The core analysis uses quantum oscillations in both MR and M vs B data, analyzing frequency shifts and effective mass changes across the compositional phase diagram.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the ability to tune electronic band structure (Dirac points) via chemical substitution provides a model for engineering topological states, which is relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in strongly correlated systems.

FIG. 2. (a) Electrical resistivity (ρ) of Y(Nb1−xTax)6Sn6 crystals for current (I) along the c-axis (I ∥[001]) and perpendicular to the c-axis (I ⊥[001]) for the x = 0.01, x = 0.30, and x = 0.64 batches. The observation that Y(Nb1−xTax)6Sn6 has smaller ρ for I ⊥[001] compared to I ∥[001] points to a reasonably large anisotropy. (b) The transverse magnetoresistance (MR) vs. magnetic field (B) for B ∥[100] and I ∥[001] at T = 2 K showing large MR response and low frequency Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) quantum oscillations demonstrate high sample quality. The relatively moderate effect of Ta substitution on transport demonstrates minimal signatures of alloy disorder in both (a) and (b).

FIG. 3. (a) Normalized resistivity of Lu1−yYy(Nb1−xTax)6Sn6 for I ⊥[001]. The Y-rich end at y = 1.00 exhibits good sample quality with minimal leveling off below ∼10 K, while samples with higher Lu concentration (e.g. y ≤0.15) show a consistent trend towards larger overall resistance ratio. Signatures of a charge density wave (CDW) emerge at y = 0.10 and evolve from a local minimum towards a kink feature by y = 0.00. FIG. 5. Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) oscillations of three sam- ples of Y(Nb1−xTax)6Sn6, extracted by plotting background- subtracted magnetoresistance ∆R (see text for details) vs in- verse magnetic field, for (a) x = 0.01, (b) x = 0.30, and (c) x = 0.64. Data fits to the Lifshitz–Kosevich formalism (see text and Table II) are shown for 2 K data (black curves). Two different frequencies, α and β, are resolvable for the x = 0.01 sample, but only the α orbit is observable for the x = 0.30 and x = 0.64 samples. A non-zero Berry phase (ϕB) manifests for all the orbits, which is consistent with a Fermi surface derived from topologically non-trivial linearly dispersing Dirac bands.
